titulo: Agent commerce and the monthly measurement loop
lead: Agents already fill in forms and compare products by reading the page the way a screen reader does. What helps is the basics done well: semantic HTML, labels, correct product data. And none of it counts without a routine: a monthly loop with the dashboards, the battery, the log and the score, always with a date.
objetivo: make forms and product pages readable for agents and set up the monthly loop for measuring in the AIs, with dates.

aprende.t: What a browser agent reads: DOM, accessibility tree, screenshot
A form with a label and autocomplete; a real button
Merchant Center and Business Profile; commerce protocols just to follow along
The monthly loop and your plan with dates

hero_alt: The owner of a leather goods store packs an online order next to the laptop.

secoes.titulo: From a readable site to the month's loop

nos.detalhe: Google's guidance (web.dev) says browser agents read the DOM, the accessibility tree (the roles, names, and states of each element), and screenshots. What works for people who use a screen reader works for the agent.

Real buttons and links (button and a elements), not generic boxes with a click handler. Each field has a label tied to it with the for attribute. No transparent layer covering what can be clicked; a layout that doesn't jump while loading.

Google's AI guide asks you to keep Merchant Center and your Google Business Profile up to date so you can appear in answers with products and places. Agent commerce protocols (UCP, which Google cites as emerging) are ones to watch, not for a small business to implement now.

Once a month, in the same week: fill in the spreadsheet, run the battery, read the log, run the score. Write down one decision only. If the appearance rate doesn't move in 3 months, look at the sources the AIs cite in your place: that's where your authority needs to exist.

secoes.legenda: The basics made readable for agents, plus a routine with a date, are worth more than any shortcut.

secoes.titulo: Four tweaks that serve people and agents
secoes.sub: Click each step. All of them come from web.dev's guide to agent-friendly sites.

texto: An action is a button, navigation is a link. If you can't use the right element, give it the correct role and tabindex.
Use a hand cursor (cursor: pointer) on what can be clicked: it's a strong signal of an action.
Every field has a visible label tied to it with the for attribute. Email, name, and phone with autocomplete: it helps the person filling in the form and helps the agent know what each field is.
No transparent layers over buttons; action elements visible and at a minimum size. A layout that doesn't move around after loading: an agent that reads a screenshot gets lost.
A correct Merchant Center feed, a clear return policy, and an up-to-date Business Profile. Follow agent commerce protocols without implementing them: sources still disagree about their status.

secoes.titulo: A readable form and the loop sheet
secoes.sub: The form is a template; the loop sheet is for copying every month.

blocos.conteudo:
<form action="/orcamento" method="post">
  <label for="nome">Name</label>
  <input id="nome" name="nome" autocomplete="name" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required>

  <label for="telefone">Phone</label>
  <input id="telefone" name="telefone" type="tel" autocomplete="tel">

  <button type="submit">Request a quote</button>
</form>

# Monthly AI loop — <month/year> (run on dd/mm/yyyy)

1. Dashboards: GSC AI impressions <n> | Bing citations <n> | cited pages <n>
2. Battery v1: appearance in the neutral questions by assistant: ChatGPT <x%> | Gemini <x%> | Perplexity <x%> | Copilot <x%>
   Sources cited in my place (top 5): <...>
3. Brand: "what is [brand]" correct in <n of 3> assistants; "who is [founder]" current in <n of 3>
4. Log: search <n> | user action <n> | training <n> | false <n> | 403 for AI bot: <yes/no>
5. Readiness score: <n> (tool and version)

Decision of the month (just one): <...>
No change for 3 months? External sources to work on: <...>

abas.html:
• A button made from a generic box with a JavaScript click handler, with no role or label.
  • A field whose label is only placeholder text inside it (it disappears when the person types).
  • Measuring once and stopping: without the next month, there's nothing to compare.

The AIV method suggests: after 3 months with no change in the battery, the lever is no longer your site's content but your presence where the AIs already look (the sources that show up in your place). Treat it as a hypothesis to test, with the loop measuring.

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after your answer.

perguntas.p: What does a browser agent use to understand a form?
opcoes: The DOM, the accessibility tree, and screenshots.
perguntas.explica: That is what the web.dev guidance says. Labels and semantic elements show up in the accessibility tree.

perguntas.p: What should a small business do about agentic commerce protocols today?
opcoes: Keep watching; for now, a correct feed in Merchant Center and an updated Business Profile are what count.
Replace the site with an app.
perguntas.explica: Google cites UCP as emerging, and sources on the others disagree. The right win is correct product data.

perguntas.p: The appearance rate in the battery has been flat for 3 months. Next step?
opcoes: Look at the sources the AIs cite in your place and work on your presence there, measuring in the loop.
perguntas.explica: The sources cited in your place show where authority needs to exist. A bought mention is inauthentic, and Google asks you to avoid it.

perguntas.p: Why does the loop have a date and one decision per month?
opcoes: Because without a date there is no comparison, and one decision per month makes it clear what changed between one measurement and the next.
perguntas.explica: A measurement without a date can't be compared; many changes at once don't tell you what worked.
